claim: Malaria is estimated to have caused 214 million clinical cases and 438,000 deaths in 2015.
source: According to the World Health Organization 2015 Malaria Report (who.int/malaria/publications/world_malaria_report/en), malaria is estimated to have caused 214 million clinical cases and 438,000 deaths in 2015.
evidence: The claim cites the World Health Organization 2015 Malaria Report as the source of these statistics.

claim: P. falciparum causes the most often fatal and medically most severe form of malaria.
source: The disease is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes and caused by parasitic protozoans of the genus Plasmodium, of which P. falciparum and P. vivax are the most prevalent and P. falciparum is causing the most often fatal and medically most severe form of malaria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about malaria pathogenesis.

claim: Debilitating clinical symptoms associated with malaria infection are caused by the multiplication of the asexual blood-stage parasites in erythrocytes.
source: Debilitating clinical symptoms associated with the infection are caused by the multiplication of the asexual blood-stage parasites in erythrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about malaria pathophysiology.

claim: Invasion of host erythrocytes by merozoites can be conceptually divided into four phases.
source: Invasion of host erythrocytes by merozoites is a complex process, conceptually divisible into four phases: (1) initial recognition of and reversible attachment to the erythrocyte membrane by the merozoite; (2) junction formation leading to irreversible attachment of the merozoite, parasitophorous vacuole formation, and release of the Plasmodium rhoptry-microneme secretory organelles; (3) invagination of the erythrocyte membrane around the merozoite, accompanied by the shedding of the merozoite's surface coat; (4) closing of the parasitophorous vacuole and resealing of the erythrocyte membrane mark the completion of merozoite invasion (Pinder et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pinder et al., 2000.

claim: P. falciparum merozoite proteins are antigenically highly diverse and in part functionally redundant.
source: In addition, P. falciparum merozoite proteins are antigenically highly diverse and in part functionally redundant, to facilitate parasite escape from host immune surveillance and to ensure erythrocyte invasion via alternative pathways (Cowman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cowman et al., 2012.

claim: Blood-stage vaccines based on merozoite surface antigens have shown limited efficacy in clinical trials.
source: Despite major efforts, blood-stage vaccines based on merozoite surface antigens have so far shown limited efficacy in clinical trials (reviewed in Halbroth and Draper, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Halbroth and Draper, 2015.

claim: Extensive antigenic polymorphism represents one major hurdle for the development of an effective blood-stage malaria vaccine.
source: Extensive antigenic polymorphism represents one major hurdle for the development of an effective blood-stage malaria vaccine (Takala et al., 2009; Dzikowski and Deitsch, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Takala et al., 2009 and Dzikowski and Deitsch, 2009.

claim: Sequencing and annotation of the P. falciparum genome has supported the identification of new blood-stage vaccine candidate antigens.
source: Sequencing and annotation of the P. falciparum genome (Gardner et al., 2002) has supported the identification of new blood-stage vaccine candidate antigens (Conway, 2015; Proietti and Doolan, 2014), among which the P. falciparum Cysteine-Rich Protective Antigen (PfCyRPA) has a number of noteworthy properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2002, Conway, 2015, and Proietti and Doolan, 2014.

claim: PfCyRPA is highly conserved among a plethora of P. falciparum isolates.
source: While PfCyRPA is highly conserved among a plethora of P. falciparum isolates, it also is poorly immunogenic in the context of natural exposure (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: PfCyRPA is poorly immunogenic in the context of natural exposure.
source: While PfCyRPA is highly conserved among a plethora of P. falciparum isolates, it also is poorly immunogenic in the context of natural exposure (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: PfCyRPA-specific monoclonal antibodies inhibit parasite growth both in vitro and in vivo by blocking merozoite invasion.
source: Moreover, PfCyRPA-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAb) inhibit parasite growth both in vitro and in vivo by blocking merozoite invasion (Dreyer et al., 2012; Favuzza et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dreyer et al., 2012 and Favuzza et al., 2016.

claim: PfCyRPA is a 42.8 kDa protein of 362 residues with a predicted N-terminal secretion signal.
source: PfCyRPA is a 42.8 kDa protein of 362 residues with a predicted N-terminal secretion signal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the protein's characteristics.

claim: Orthologs of PfCyRPA have been found in the genomes of P. vivax, P. knowlesi, P. cynomolgi, and P. reichenowi.
source: Orthologs of PfCyRPA have been found in the genomes of the human malaria parasite P. vivax and the primate pathogens P. knowlesi, P. cynomolgi, and P. reichenowi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but not in the sequenced genomes of other Plasmodium species.
evidence: The claim references Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing sequence alignment of CyRPA orthologs.

claim: P. falciparum PfCyRPA shares on average 42% sequence identity with its orthologs.
source: P. falciparum PfCyRPA shares on average 42% sequence identity with its orthologs, but within different P. falciparum isolates PfCyRPA is highly conserved: just 13 dimorphic amino acid positions (highlighted in Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were found in 227 P. falciparum field isolates (Manske et al., 2012), and only a single variant (Arg399 instead of Ser399) was found at a frequency of greater than 2%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Manske et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Just 13 dimorphic amino acid positions were found in 227 P. falciparum field isolates.
source: P. falciparum PfCyRPA shares on average 42% sequence identity with its orthologs, but within different P. falciparum isolates PfCyRPA is highly conserved: just 13 dimorphic amino acid positions (highlighted in Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were found in 227 P. falciparum field isolates (Manske et al., 2012), and only a single variant (Arg399 instead of Ser399) was found at a frequency of greater than 2%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Manske et al., 2012.

claim: PfCyRPA is part of a multi-protein complex including PfRipr and PfRH5.
source: PfCyRPA is part of a multi-protein complex (Reddy et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016) including also the PfRH5-interacting protein PfRipr and the reticulocyte binding-like homologous protein PfRH5, which binds to the erythrocyte receptor basigin (Baum et al., 2009; Crosnier et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016; Baum et al., 2009; Crosnier et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b, 2014.

claim: PfRH5 binds to the erythrocyte receptor basigin.
source: PfCyRPA is part of a multi-protein complex (Reddy et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016) including also the PfRH5-interacting protein PfRipr and the reticulocyte binding-like homologous protein PfRH5, which binds to the erythrocyte receptor basigin (Baum et al., 2009; Crosnier et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2009; Crosnier et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b, 2014.

claim: PfRH5, PfCyRPA, and PfRipr colocalize during parasite invasion at the junction between merozoites and erythrocytes.
source: PfRH5, PfCyRPA, and PfRipr colocalize during parasite invasion at the junction between merozoites and erythrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a direct observation.

claim: The PfRH5-PfCyRPA-PfRipr complex is required for triggering Ca2+ release and establishment of tight junctions.
source: The complex seems to be required both for triggering Ca2+ release and establishment of tight junctions (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: Merozoites deficient in PfCyRPA or PfRH5 can still bind to erythrocytes but do not attach irreversibly and cannot invade the host cells.
source: While merozoites deficient in PfCyRPA or PfRH5 can still bind to erythrocytes, they do not attach irreversibly and cannot invade the host cells (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: PfRH5 induces invasion-blocking antibodies that are effective across common genetic variants.
source: Like PfCyRPA (Dreyer et al., 2012), PfRH5 induces invasion-blocking antibodies that are effective across common genetic variants (Douglas et al., 2011; Bustamante et al., 2013; Douglas et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Douglas et al., 2011; Bustamante et al., 2013; Douglas et al., 2014.

claim: The crystal structures of PfRH5 in complex with basigin and neutralizing inhibitory mAb have been determined.
source: To this end, the crystal structures of PfRH5 in complex with basigin and neutralizing inhibitory mAb have been determined (Chen et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014 and Wright et al., 2014.

claim: The 16 anti-PfCyRPA mAbs showed six distinctive reactivity patterns with seven overlapping recombinant protein fragments of PfCyRPA.
source: The 16 anti-PfCyRPA mAbs available for analysis (Dreyer et al., 2012; Favuzza et al., 2016), showed six distinctive reactivity patterns with seven overlapping recombinant protein fragments of PfCyRPA, assigning them to the epitope groups A – F, with groups A, B, C, and F comprising the parasite inhibitory and groups D and E the non-inhibitory mAbs (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and citations to Dreyer et al., 2012 and Favuzza et al., 2016.

claim: Epitope groups A, B, C, and F comprise parasite inhibitory mAbs while groups D and E comprise non-inhibitory mAbs.
source: The 16 anti-PfCyRPA mAbs available for analysis (Dreyer et al., 2012; Favuzza et al., 2016), showed six distinctive reactivity patterns with seven overlapping recombinant protein fragments of PfCyRPA, assigning them to the epitope groups A – F, with groups A, B, C, and F comprising the parasite inhibitory and groups D and E the non-inhibitory mAbs (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: All anti-PfCyRPA mAbs bound to the full-length PfCyRPA (fragment 1).
source: All mAbs bound to the full-length PfCyRPA (without the signal sequence; fragment 1).
evidence: This is stated as a direct observation from the binding experiments.

claim: Epitope group A mAbs recognize conformational epitopes not present in any of the shorter PfCyRPA sequence stretches.
source: mAbs belonging to epitope group A exclusively bound this fragment, indicating that they recognize conformational epitopes not present in any of the shorter PfCyRPA sequence stretches.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding pattern observed in the experiments.

claim: Anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb and anti-PfRH5 BS1.2 mAb at 250 µg/mL inhibited P. falciparum 3D7 growth by 21% ± 2.2% and 31% ± 4.6%, respectively.
source: while mAbs c12 and BS1.2 at a concentration of 250 µg/mL inhibited growth by 21% ± 2.2% and 31% ± 4.6%, respectively, the combination of both mAbs (250 µg/mL each) inhibited growth by 59% ± 1.4%; (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The combination of anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb and anti-PfRH5 BS1.2 mAb (250 µg/mL each) inhibited P. falciparum 3D7 growth by 59% ± 1.4%.
source: while mAbs c12 and BS1.2 at a concentration of 250 µg/mL inhibited growth by 21% ± 2.2% and 31% ± 4.6%, respectively, the combination of both mAbs (250 µg/mL each) inhibited growth by 59% ± 1.4%; (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Differences in parasite growth inhibition between mAbs c12 and BS1.2 alone and their combinations are statistically significant.
source: Differences in parasite growth inhibition between mAbs c12 and BS1.2 alone and their combinations are statistically significant (unpaired t test with Welch's correction, 95% confidence interval, two-tailed p value).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In NODscidIL2Rγnull mice, parasitemia in control groups reached 19.6% ± 0.8% on day 9 after mAb injection.
source: In the control groups, parasitemia reached 19.6% ± 0.8% on day 9 after mAb injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the in vivo study.

claim: In NODscidIL2Rγnull mice, 2.5 mg of c12 or BS1.2 mAb limited parasitemia to 2.2 ± 0.5% and 2% ± 0.3% respectively on day nine after mAb injection.
source: Parasitemia in mice having received 2.5 mg c12 or BS1.2 mAb increased only marginally, reaching 2.2 ± 0.5 and 2% ± 0.3% on day nine after mAb injection, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the in vivo study.

claim: At 0.5 mg dose, c12 and BS1.2 mAbs inhibited parasite growth to 10.1 ± 2.3% and 10.8% ± 6.9% parasitemia, respectively.
source: At the lower dose of 0.5 mg c12 and BS1.2 inhibited parasite growth to 10.1 ± 2.3 and 10.8% ± 6.9% parasitemia, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Parasitemia decreased significantly (p=0.0356) and reached only 4.8% ± 1.9% on day 9 when mice received 0.5 mg of both anti-PfRH5 BS1.2 mAb and anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb.
source: In accord with the in vitro data, parasitemia decreased significantly (p=0.0356; unpaired t test, 95% confidence interval, two-tailed) and reached only 4.8% ± 1.9% on day 9 if mice received 0.5 mg of the anti-PfRH5 BS1.2 mAb in addition to 0.5 mg of the anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The far-UV CD spectrum of PfCyRPA is consistent with an all-β structure connected by loop regions and the absence of α-helices.
source: The far-UV CD spectrum of PfCyRPA is consistent with an all-β structure connected by loop regions and the absence of α-helices (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mass spectrometric analysis of proteolytic fragments of PfCyRPA revealed at least four disulfide bonds that are sequential along the sequence.
source: Mass spectrometric analysis of proteolytic fragments of PfCyRPA revealed at least four disulfide bonds that are sequential along the sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The two Trp residues present in PfCyRPA are buried in the native state.
source: Intrinsic fluorescence showed that the two Trp residues present in PfCyRPA are buried in the native state.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence spectroscopy data.

claim: Addition of 50 mM reducing agent had no significant effect on the fluorescence of PfCyRPA.
source: Also, the disulfide bonds seem to be buried, because addition of 50 mM reducing agent had no significant effect on the fluorescence of PfCyRPA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: PfCyRPA forms a compact, disulfide-stabilized molecule of predominantly β-sheet structure.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with PfCyRPA forming a compact, disulfide-stabilized molecule of predominantly β-sheet structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the biophysical characterization data (CD, mass spectrometry, fluorescence).

claim: The crystal structure of PfCyRPA was determined to a resolution of 2.5 Å.
source: The crystal structure of PfCyRPA, determined to a resolution of 2.5 Å (detailed in Supplementary file 1), confirmed our biophysical analyses (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: PfCyRPA adopts a six-bladed β-propeller structure.
source: PfCyRPA adopts a six-bladed β-propeller structure that buries the disulfide bonds and the Trp residues.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure determination.

claim: Each blade of the PfCyRPA propeller is constructed by a four-stranded anti-parallel β-sheet.
source: Each blade of the propeller is constructed by a four-stranded anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The five disulfide bonds in PfCyRPA are located within blades 2–6.
source: The five disulfide bonds in PfCyRPA are located within blades 2–6 (Figure 3A), stabilizing each individual blade.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The first blade of PfCyRPA has no disulfide bond and is formed by β-strands from the N- and C-terminal regions.
source: The first blade has no disulfide bond; it is formed by β-strands from the N- and C-terminal regions of PfCyRPA, potentially enabling conformational changes in PfCyRPA by opening and closing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure and includes speculation about potential conformational changes.

claim: The closest structural relative of PfCyRPA is the catalytic domain of Vibrio cholerae sialidase.
source: The closest structural relative is the catalytic domain of Vibrio cholerae sialidase (Moustafa et al., 2004) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison and citation to Moustafa et al., 2004.

claim: PfCyRPA and Vibrio cholerae sialidase have only 9% sequence identity and structures with a large rmsd of 3.7 Å over 285 residues.
source: The two proteins have only 9% sequence identity and the structures have a large root mean square distance (rmsd) of 3.7 Å over 285 residues, clearly showing that while the overall fold is similar, the structures are very different with respect to the inclination of the blades (Figure 3C) and the length and conformations of the surface loops connecting the β-strands (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: PfCyRPA contains a signature sequence motif for sialidases known as an Asp-box (201-SHDKGETW-208).
source: PfCyRPA also contains a signature sequence motif for sialidases known as an Asp-box (201-SHDKGETW-208; conserved residues are underlined) (Roggentin et al., 1989), which serve structural roles in the β-propellers of sialidases.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and citation to Roggentin et al., 1989.

claim: PfCyRPA contains only a single Asp-box while bacterial sialidases contain between three to five Asp-boxes.
source: However, while bacterial sialidases contain between three to five Asp-boxes, PfCyRPA contains only a single one.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Two molecules of PfCyRPA are present in the asymmetric unit and have conformational differences in several surface loops.
source: Two molecules of PfCyRPA are present in the asymmetric unit and have conformational differences in several surface loops, suggesting possible flexibility of these loops in solution (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PfCyRPA has no sialidase activity.
source: We detected no sialidase activity, however, when we tested recombinant PfCyRPA for neuraminidase activity using a colorimetric assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: PfCyRPA contains none of the residues necessary for sialidase catalysis.
source: PfCyRPA contains none of the residues necessary for catalysis, nor does it harbor a Ca2+ binding site, providing structural correlates of the absence of sialidase activity in PfCyRPA.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis comparing PfCyRPA to known sialidases.

claim: PfCyRPA does not harbor a Ca2+ binding site.
source: PfCyRPA contains none of the residues necessary for catalysis, nor does it harbor a Ca2+ binding site, providing structural correlates of the absence of sialidase activity in PfCyRPA.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis.

claim: PfCyRPA and sialidases may have evolved from a common ancestor, or PfCyRPA could have evolved from a genuine sialidase to adopt other functionalities.
source: PfCyRPA and sialidases may have evolved from a common ancestor, or PfCyRPA could have evolved from a genuine sialidase to adopt other functionalities.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary relationships.

claim: The parasite inhibitory anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb binds tightly to PfCyRPA with a Kd of ca. 1 nM.
source: The parasite inhibitory anti-PfCyRPA c12 mAb binds tightly to PfCyRPA with a Kd of ca. 1 nM as determined by surface plasmon resonance analysis (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface plasmon resonance data cited from Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: mAb c12 recognizes PfCyRPA independent of its glycosylation.
source: This mAb recognizes PfCyRPA independent of its glycosylation, as revealed by Western blot analyses (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Three different crystal forms of c12 Fab were obtained containing a total of four crystallographically independent Fab molecules.
source: We obtained three different crystal forms containing a total of four crystallographically independent Fab molecules.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the crystallographic results.

claim: Superposition of the c12 Fab structures showed very little structural plasticity of the CDR loops.
source: Superposition of the structures showed very little structural plasticity of the CDR loops (Figure 4C), suggesting that they retain their structures upon epitope binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The crystal structure of the PfCyRPA/c12 complex was determined at a resolution of 4.0 Å.
source: We determined the crystal structure of the PfCyRPA/c12 complex at a resolution of 4.0 Å by molecular replacement using the individual high-resolution structures of c12 and PfCyRPA as search models (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is a surface composed of blade two and part of blade 3 of PfCyRPA.
source: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is a surface composed of blade two and part of blade 3 of PfCyRPA (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure of the complex shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The most frequent amino acid dimorphism of PfCyRPA at position 339 is located outside the epitope recognized by mAb c12.
source: The most frequent amino acid dimorphism of PfCyRPA at position 339 is thus located outside the epitope recognized by mAb c12, consistent with the observation that mAb c12 binds to P. falciparum independent of the PfCyRPA variant they express (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and cited observation from Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: mAb c12 buries a total surface area of 950 Å2 on PfCyRPA.
source: mAb c12 buries a total surface area of 950 Å2 on PfCyRPA with the major contributor being the light chain, which buries 520 Å2, while the heavy chain buries only 430 Å2.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the complex.

claim: The c12 light chain buries 520 Å2 on PfCyRPA while the heavy chain buries 430 Å2.
source: mAb c12 buries a total surface area of 950 Å2 on PfCyRPA with the major contributor being the light chain, which buries 520 Å2, while the heavy chain buries only 430 Å2.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the complex.

claim: The surface complementarity coefficient Sc of the PfCyRPA/c12 complex is 0.67.
source: The surface complementarity coefficient Sc of the complex is 0.67, a typical value for antibody-antigen interactions (Lawrence and Colman, 1993); a value of one would denote perfect complementarity.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and comparison to typical values cited from Lawrence and Colman, 1993.

claim: Seven hydrogen bonds are possible between PfCyRPA and the c12 light chain.
source: Seven hydrogen bonds are possible between PfCyRPA and the c12 light chain.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the complex.

claim: A salt bridge between PfCyRPA residue Asp66 and CDR1 residue Arg50 contributes to complex stability.
source: A particularly large contribution to complex stability may stem from a salt bridge between PfCyRPA residue Asp66 and CDR1 residue Arg50, which by mutagenesis was found to be true (see below), a further confirmation that the PfCyRPA/c12 complex structure is correct.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: mAb c12 recognizes a discontinuous epitope that contains at least 17 residues distributed over four PfCyRPA sequence stretches.
source: What is clear from the structure is that mAb c12 recognizes a discontinuous epitope that contains at least 17 residues distributed over four PfCyRPA sequence stretches (marked in Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the complex.

claim: The Asp66Lys replacement significantly reduced binding of mAb c12 to PfCyRPA.
source: When Asp66 was changed to Lys, a capture ELISA detected significantly weaker binding of the mAb c12 to the Asp66Lys variant of PfCyRPA (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Asp66Lys replacement did not affect binding of the control mAb SB1.6.
source: As expected, the Asp66Lys replacement did not affect binding of the control mAb SB1.6 (Figure 6B), which belongs to the unrelated epitope group F and is expected to engage in crucial interactions with PfCyRPA residues located between residues 181 and 251 (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PfCyRPA has been identified as a novel malaria blood-stage vaccine target.
source: PfCyRPA has been identified as a novel malaria blood-stage vaccine target in an endeavor to test predicted P. falciparum open reading frames for the capacity to elicit parasite-inhibitory mAbs (Dreyer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dreyer et al., 2010.

claim: PfCyRPA is stage-specifically expressed in late schizonts.
source: PfCyRPA is stage-specifically expressed in late schizonts and elicits mAbs that inhibit parasite growth in vitro and in a P. falciparum experimental infection model based on NODscidIL2Rγnull mice engrafted with human erythrocytes (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: Antibodies against PfRH5 and PfCyRPA have additive parasite growth inhibitory activity.
source: Here, we show that antibodies against PfRH5 and PfCyRPA have additive parasite growth inhibitory activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the in vitro and in vivo experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inclusion of both PfCyRPA and PfRH5 into a multivalent subunit vaccine represents an attractive strategy to prevent emergence of escape mutants.
source: Inclusion of both antigens into a multivalent subunit vaccine therefore represents an attractive strategy to prevent emergence of escape mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive inhibitory effects observed.

claim: An ortholog of PfCyRPA is present in the genome of P. vivax.
source: While an ortholog of PfCyRPA is also present in the genome of the human parasite P. vivax, an ortholog of PfRH5 has only been found so far in the genome of P. reichenowi, a chimpanzee malaria parasite closely related to P. falciparum (Otto et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Otto et al., 2014.

claim: An ortholog of PfRH5 has only been found in the genome of P. reichenowi.
source: While an ortholog of PfCyRPA is also present in the genome of the human parasite P. vivax, an ortholog of PfRH5 has only been found so far in the genome of P. reichenowi, a chimpanzee malaria parasite closely related to P. falciparum (Otto et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Otto et al., 2014.

claim: The distribution of orthologs may indicate a function of PfCyRPA beyond its role as a protein-binding platform in the ternary complex with PfRH5 and PfRipr.
source: This may indicate a function of PfCyRPA beyond its role as a protein-binding platform in the ternary complex with PfRH5 and PfRipr.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the distribution of orthologs.

claim: Recent results are not consistent with the suggestion that PfCyRPA anchors the ternary complex through a GPI anchor to the parasite membrane.
source: While it has been claimed that PfCyRPA anchors the ternary complex through a GPI anchor to the parasite membrane (Reddy et al., 2015), recent results are not consistent with this suggestion (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2015 and Volz et al., 2016.

claim: Additional proteins might be involved in anchoring the complex to the parasite membrane.
source: This inconsistency suggests that additional proteins might be involved in anchoring the complex to the parasite membrane and that PfCyRPA has an essential function other than that of an anchor.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the inconsistency noted.

claim: The five sequential disulfide bonds of PfCyRPA are in blades 1–5, leaving blade 6 without local stabilization.
source: In this context, it may be relevant that the five sequential disulfide bonds of PfCyRPA are in blades 1–5, leaving blade 6 of the β-propeller structure without such a local stabilization.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis.

claim: Blade six of PfCyRPA could act as a gate to allow conformational changes.
source: Blade six is constructed by β-strands from the N- and the C-terminus, and in principle could act as a gate to allow PfCyRPA to undergo substantial conformational changes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural features.

claim: Structural vaccinology defines epitopes from antigen-antibody complex crystal structures and allows the design of surrogate antigens that elicit protective humoral immune responses.
source: Structural vaccinology defines epitopes from antigen-antibody complex crystal structures and thus allows the design of surrogate antigens that elicit protective humoral immune responses.
evidence: This is stated as an established approach in vaccine development.

claim: Both PfCyRPA and PfRH5 elicit protective as well as non-protective antibodies.
source: Both PfCyRPA and PfRH5 elicit protective as well as non-protective antibodies (Dreyer et al., 2012; Douglas et al., 2011), making them candidates for structure-based approaches, that aim to focus the immune responses on protective epitopes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dreyer et al., 2012 and Douglas et al., 2011.

claim: The crystal structure of the protective mAb c12 bound to PfCyRPA provides an ideal starting point for the design of a conformationally stabilized PfCyRPA-derived peptide antigen.
source: Even at the comparatively moderate resolution of 4 Å, the crystal structure of the protective mAb c12 bound to PfCyRPA provides an ideal starting point for the design of a conformationally stabilized PfCyRPA-derived peptide antigen to elicit primarily protective antibodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data obtained.

claim: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is monomorphic.
source: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is monomorphic and, like PfCyRPA in general, little immunogenic in the natural context.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis and sequence conservation data.

claim: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is little immunogenic in the natural context.
source: The epitope recognized by mAb c12 is monomorphic and, like PfCyRPA in general, little immunogenic in the natural context.
evidence: This is stated based on previous observations about PfCyRPA immunogenicity.

claim: Focusing the vaccine-induced immune response on the c12 epitope may confer a strong protective effect.
source: Focusing the vaccine-induced immune response on this PfCyRPA epitope may confer a strong protective effect.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential vaccine design.

claim: Malaria vaccine candidates based on single-antigens have been uniformly unsuccessful.
source: Malaria vaccine candidates based on single-antigens have been uniformly unsuccessful and an effective subunit vaccine will likely have to include antigens from more than one stage of the parasite life cycle (pre-erythrocytic, liver stage, and blood stage components), as well as sexual blood-stage gametocyte or mosquito-stage parasite antigens as transmission-blocking components.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about malaria vaccine development.

claim: The Plasmodium genome contains more than 5000 open reading frames of which only <0.5% have been tested as vaccine candidates.
source: The Plasmodium genome contains more than 5000 open reading frames of which only <0.5% have been tested as vaccine candidates, so careful selection of new targets for an optimized multi-valent vaccine is called for (Proietti and Doolan, 2014; Dups et al., 2014; Longley et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Proietti and Doolan, 2014; Dups et al., 2014; Longley et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015.

claim: PfCyRPA represents one of the most promising new blood-stage vaccine candidate antigens identified with the support of –omics approaches.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Halbroth and Draper, 2015.

claim: A structure-based approach for malaria vaccine development is now possible with the availability of structural analyses for both PfCyRPA and PfRH5 in complex with inhibitory antibodies.
